Replace the justification by "choose a well-sampled reference level, so that the contrasts are estimated precisely (the same data, same model, but different, more precise comparisons)". head: **Medium · 2C-RandomEffects.qmd:295** (N-g2-04)
body: **Problem:** "...because REML estimates the REs conditional on the fixed effects, REML likelihoods are not directly comparable if fixed effects are changed." This is not the reason and contradicts l.279 (REML integrates the fixed effects out). The REML likelihood is the likelihood of error contrasts that are defined by the fixed-effect design matrix; when the fixed-effect structure changes, the contrasts, and thus the data the likelihood refers to, change, so the two likelihoods are not likelihoods of the same data.

**Evidence:** standard theory (Pinheiro and Bates 2000; Verbyla 2019, which the chapter cites at l.688). Also in lme4, `AIC()`/`logLik()` of REML fits with different fixed effects are numerically computable but not comparable.

**Proposed solution:** Replace the clause by: "because the REML likelihood is based on the part of the data that is free of the fixed effects, so it refers to different data when the fixed-effect structure changes, REML likelihoods are not comparable between models with different fixed effects." Fits together with the REML box proposed in R089.
**Relation to existing issues:** extends R089 (R089 handles the structure and ML-vs-REML rule, not this incorrect explanation)

**Assessment round 3:** REAL · fix: DIRECT · solution: BEST — 2C ~295: "because REML estimates the REs conditional on the fixed effects, REML likelihoods are not directly comparable" is not the reason and contradicts ~279 (REML integrates the fixed effects out); the REML likelihood is the likelihood of error contrasts defined by the fixed-effect design, i.e. of different data when the fixed effects change. Verified that anova() refits with ML (R089).

**Exact fix (round 3):** old "The reason is that, because REML estimates the REs conditional on the fixed effects, REML likelihoods are not directly comparable if fixed effects are changed. I would recommend sticking to this, although I have to say that I have always wondered how big this problem is, compared to the other df problems associated to mixed models (see @sec-re-df)." ⇒ "The reason is that the REML likelihood refers to the part of the data that is free of the fixed effects, i.e. to different data when the fixed-effect structure changes, so REML likelihoods are not comparable between models with different fixed effects. For models with identical fixed effects (e.g. when comparing RE structures), REML is fine."

**Applied 2026-10-04 (awaiting check):** reason clause replaced ("the REML likelihood refers to linear combinations of the data that do not depend on the fixed effects (@sec-re-reml), i.e. to different data when the fixed-effect structure changes"); the "always wondered" remark was kept (Florian's voice; consider dropping it, it undercuts the rule).

head: **Medium · 6C-CaseStudies.qmd:820-826** (N-g5-15)
body: **Problem:** "What about the germination temperatures, T50/T95? They could be mediators, Seed Shape -> T95 -> SBDensity, so it is up to if you want to include them or not!" The book's causal chapter teaches that this is not a free choice: adjusting for a mediator removes the indirect effect, i.e. changes the estimand (total versus direct effect), and can induce bias if there are unmeasured mediator-outcome confounders. The scientific question here is the effect of seed traits on seed bank density, which is a total-effect question, for which mediators should be left out.
**Evidence:** 3B (@sec-causal-framework); consistent with the preceding line where only confounders (Altitude, Humidity) were added.

**Proposed solution:** "T50/T95 are possible mediators (Seed Shape -> T95 -> SBDensity). If we want the total effect of the seed traits we must not include them, because adjusting for a mediator removes the part of the effect that goes through it; include them only if the question is the direct effect (and then be aware of mediator-outcome confounding, @sec-causal-framework)."

**Assessment round 3:** REAL · fix: DIRECT · solution: BEST — 6C:826 "They could be mediators ..., so it is up to if you want to include them or not!" contradicts 3B (adjusting for a mediator changes the estimand)

**Exact fix (round 3):** old: "They could be mediators (@sec-causal-framework), Seed Shape -\\> T95 -\\> SBDensity, so it is up to if you want to include them or not!" ⇒ "They are possible mediators (Seed Shape -\\> T95 -\\> SBDensity). If we want the total effect of the seed traits, we must not include them, because adjusting for a mediator removes the part of the effect that goes through it; include them only if the question is the direct effect (and then be aware of mediator-outcome confounding, @sec-causal-framework)."

**Applied 2026-10-04 (awaiting check):** shorter wording: "They could be mediators (Seed Shape -> T95 -> SBDensity).
